stories.title: Nvidia Closes the Southeast Asian Back Door to China
stories.story:
For two years, the architecture of the global AI arms race rested on a quiet fiction: American chips could not legally go to China, but they could go to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia — and Chinese hyperscalers could simply rent compute time there remotely. The fiction has now collapsed.

Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, to stop shipping AI servers to all four countries while it audits compliance with new US export rules issued earlier this month. The Commerce Department simultaneously opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia partner, for allegedly funneling advanced chips onward to China. A separate entity, Airvres — formerly operating under the Inspur name, a firm already on the federal blocklist — reportedly moved at least $5.6 billion in chips through Southeast Asia between 2024 and 2026.

The numbers reveal why the loophole mattered so much. Nvidia's Singapore arm alone booked roughly $104 billion in 2025 revenue, a figure that bundled significant China-linked business. And according to the think tank Institute for Progress, remote data centers in these four countries supplied roughly 24% of China's total AI computing power — a dependency that one stroke of Commerce Department rulemaking has now put at risk.

The downstream effects are immediate. Moonshot AI canceled a $150 million Blackwell chip order. Z.AI's GLM-5.5 model is delayed until Q1 2027. The gap between Chinese and American frontier AI capability, already measured in months, is widening. What was once a war over chip design is becoming a war over geography — and Washington has just redrawn the map.
stories.hook: The chip embargo on China didn't fail; it just had the wrong address.

stories.title: SAP's Second 10,000-Job Purge in Three Years
stories.story:
Europe's most valuable software company is preparing to cut at least 10,000 jobs — roughly 9% of its global workforce — in what would be its second restructuring of this scale in under three years. The last round, begun in January 2024, cost approximately €3.1 billion and was sold as a one-time pivot toward AI. This time, CEO Christian Klein is making the same argument with no apology for the repetition.

The mechanism is straightforward and worth understanding clearly. SAP sells enterprise software — the systems that run payroll, procurement, and supply chains for the world's largest corporations. For decades, those systems required armies of human consultants and SAP's own engineers to configure, maintain, and sell. Klein's bet is that AI agents, specifically SAP's Joule suite, can absorb much of that labor directly inside the product. If the agent handles the configuration, you no longer need as many people in product, engineering, or sales — the three departments Bloomberg says face the deepest cuts.

What makes this consequential beyond the headcount is the structural signal it sends. SAP negotiated an employment guarantee with Germany's labor council through 2028, meaning the cuts will fall disproportionately outside Germany — in the U.S., India, and elsewhere. And this is happening against a backdrop where U.S. employers cited AI in roughly one in five job-cut announcements through October 2026. SAP isn't a struggling company doing this under duress; it just completed four acquisitions this year and posted a strong quarter. The cuts are a choice about what kind of company generates value going forward: one where humans write and sell software, or one where AI does both and humans oversee the margins.
stories.hook: When the company that sells AI transformation software has to restructure twice in three years to afford it, the technology is cannibalizing its own sales force.

stories.title: Europe Bets €50 Billion to Stop Its Tech Companies Leaving
stories.story:
The pattern has been consistent for a decade: a European quantum or AI startup raises a seed round in Paris or Munich, runs out of growth capital at scale, and sells to an American acquirer or relocates to Silicon Valley. The European Commission is now trying to close that specific exit door.

On November 25, the Commission proposed its first-ever Quantum Act alongside a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund sized at up to €50 billion — structured not as grants but as equity and equity-like financing, managed with the European Investment Bank. The distinction matters. Grants flow in and get spent. Equity investments return capital if the bet pays off and, critically, give a public backer a seat at the table when an acquirer comes knocking.

The numbers reveal the problem the fund is designed to solve. Europe hosts roughly a third of the world's quantum companies and last year spent €8.6 billion in public quantum funding — more than the United States' €5.3 billion. Yet private venture investment in European quantum startups was just €1.1 billion, against €7 billion in the US. Public money has been seeding the garden; private money has been harvesting it elsewhere.

The €50 billion figure is an ambition, not a check: the fund is designed to leverage €400–500 billion in total public and private investment and won't launch until the EU's next budget cycle begins in 2028. The legislation still must clear EU member states and the European Parliament. What's already law is the procurement component — restricting public quantum tenders to EU-controlled or reciprocal-partner suppliers, borrowing directly from the Chips Act playbook.

The implied next move is a race for position. American and Chinese firms with European subsidiaries will now audit whether their ownership structures qualify them for procurement. European startups have a new argument in every VC pitch deck: a captive government customer base is now legally encoded.
stories.hook: Europe has been great at growing quantum companies and terrible at keeping them — this is the first time it's tried to fix the second problem with money rather than rhetoric.
stories.source: Reuters / European Commission COM(2026) 965 / Quantum Computing Report

stories.title: The World's Largest IPO Is Already Under Water
stories.story:
On November 19, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share — the largest public offering in history, raising $81.3 billion. The stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq, briefly carrying a valuation north of $2 trillion, and the AI faithful celebrated. Five trading days later, the stock was trading at $73.85: 11 percent below the issue price, and down more than 30 percent from its opening-day peak.

The mechanics of the collapse matter. Underwriters exercised their full greenshoe option — the standard mechanism that lets banks buy back shares to stabilize a falling stock — after just a single day of trading, injecting $12.2 billion into the deal's proceeds but, in doing so, exhausting their main price-support tool almost immediately. Once the greenshoe is gone, there is no floor. When the broader AI selloff hit Nvidia, Alphabet, and SoftBank simultaneously, Anthropic had no cushion left.

The deeper problem is structural. Anthropic burns capital at a ferocious rate to train and run frontier models, and open-source rivals are delivering roughly 80–90 percent of that capability at a fraction of the cost. Public investors, unlike venture capitalists, cannot easily ignore the question of when the revenue catches the infrastructure bill. The Amodei siblings' disclosure that they each sold roughly $280 million in shares at the IPO — standard, technically, but poorly timed optically — compounded the unease.

What this implies for December is significant. Some 303 million locked-up shares become eligible for sale in the coming weeks. With S&P placing Nvidia on downgrade watch over its own circular AI-financing arrangements, and Anthropic's slide reframing the whole sector, every AI lab watching its own IPO window — including OpenAI — now has a live cautionary tale to price against.
stories.hook: The largest IPO ever went underwater in five days — not because the technology failed, but because the market finally asked what it costs.

stories.title: An Italian Bank Seizes the Keys to Germany's Second-Largest Lender
stories.story:
For two years, UniCredit's Andrea Orcel has been running the most audacious hostile takeover in European banking since the financial crisis. On Thursday it was over. Poland's financial regulator KNF — the final gatekeeper — issued its approval, clearing the path because Commerzbank owns 69 percent of Poland's mBank. Within hours, UniCredit filed a demand for an extraordinary shareholder meeting to replace nine of the ten shareholder-side seats on Commerzbank's supervisory board, and nominated Orcel himself as chairman.

The mechanism is surgical: UniCredit does not yet own an absolute majority, but after its July share-exchange offer it will hold roughly 47.6 percent of voting rights once settlement completes on December 7. At a shareholder meeting, that is enough to elect an entirely new oversight board — which then appoints management. Control without crossing 50 percent is deliberate: Polish law would trigger a mandatory full buyout offer for mBank above that threshold, an obligation UniCredit has calculated it cannot afford.

The German government's resistance collapsed last week when Berlin dropped its demand for two reserved supervisory board seats in exchange for UniCredit's pledge to keep Commerzbank listed and headquartered in Frankfurt. Jens Weidmann, the former Bundesbank president who chairs the board being swept away, is now left to manage an orderly handover to the man who surprised him with an unsolicited stake purchase back in September 2024.

What this implies: a combined UniCredit-Commerzbank would become the eurozone's third-largest bank by assets. The harder question is for Germany's Mittelstand, which has long relied on Commerzbank as its relationship lender. If Orcel optimises for pan-European returns and cross-border synergies, lending to mid-sized German manufacturers — the ones not glamorous enough for Deutsche Bank — may quietly shrink.
stories.hook: UniCredit just proved you can take over a country's second-biggest bank without ever owning a majority of it.
